newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Egypt's Copts survive as religious minority.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Egypt's Copts survive as religious minority.

text.p: A herd of camels lopes down the dusty main road in the Cairo suburb of Imbaba, adding to the chaos of honking taxis, a rowdy wedding procession and flocks of goats swarming over mounds of uncollected garbage.

In Imbaba's teeming streets, it is easy to miss the discreet signs of a Coptic minority -- the cross above a doorway, pictures of Christ in a pharmacy and the voices of children singing hymns in ancient Coptic language that few understand.
"I've memorised the letters but I don't know the meaning," said 22-year-old Assam, a student, reading from a bilingual Coptic-Arabic prayer book at Mar Mina Church.
Like Latin for Roman Catholics, the Coptic language has largely retreated from the lives and liturgy of the Arabic speaking Copts in Egypt, where the official religion is Islam.
But as a token in traditional church rituals it serves to cement the native Christian community of Egypt in a country where they compose about 10 percent of the 60 million people.
"That preserves the service and the identity," said Yousriya Loza Sawiris, one of the few Copts in Egypt's parliament.

Religious and secular leaders see preserving Coptic identity as one of the challenges for the "Mother Church of Africa", which this month marked the silver anniversary of its independent pope, Shenouda III.
They speak of a need for practical leadership, of low government representation, red tape in building or renovating churches, and tales of sectarian violence.

"Very grim. The future is very grim. Not because we are expecting Islamic law but that the Copts are living with the condition of being a second-class community," said Milad Hanna, columnist and chairman of the non-governmental Coptic Society.
"Hence they do not breed leaders, only bishops or popes. We need leaders without a black turban," he said in an interview.
COPTS WERE WEAKENED THROUGHOUT CENTURIES

The church of the Copts was the first in Africa when it was set up in the first century AD and was known for monasticism and fasting. Copts were a majority until well after Islam came in the 7th century and Coptic was a language of the streets until about the 13th century.
Outside its birthplace the modern Coptic church has spread to Europe, the United States, Africa, the Middle East and the Gulf.
But Moslem fundamentalism and a legal relic of Ottoman rule which requires a presidential decree for Copts to build or renew churches has at times shackled Orthodox activity at home.
Hanna showed Reuters a copy of a letter he co-authored in April asking the Justice Ministry to abolish the need for the presidential decree.
He said he has been seeking for three years to set up a church in the northern town of Marina, where he is mayor.
Clutching a cross in one hand and a microphone in the other, Pope Shenouda III spoke to journalists in Alexandria last month about the church he has headed for the past 25 years.
Church bells tolled in the background. Across the courtyard in the darkened interior of St Mark's Cathedral, worshippers bowed their heads in prayer in front of lighted candles.
Shenouda said the community was going from strength to strength but had to keep a low profile on its own turf.
"We have built many new churches...but we don't write about them in newspapers in order not to have a bad reaction among the fanatic Moslems," said the pope, surrounded by priests in black.

Asked about reports of discrimination and forced conversions to Islam, Shenouda said: "I want to say to you that Islamic groups in Egypt are very dangerous and very aggressive, not only against Christians but also against the government itself.
"The problem is a problem of the spirit among the common people," he said. "For this reason most of the Copts were not elected in the parliament."
COPTS ARE SECOND-CLASS CITIZENS IN EGYPT

As doctors, lawyers and business people, Copts are thriving in Egypt's economy but are less active in government. Two junior ministers are Copts and the only Coptic members of the 454-seat parliament are among the 10 appointed by President Hosni Mubarak to dilute the dominant element -- Moslem men.
"An appointed Coptic member of parliament should behave, he should not speak much, never oppose the government and behave in a decorative way," Hanna said.
But Sawiris said: "I have never in my whole life been stopped because I was a Christian."
"My first goal is not that the Copts may have authority, but that the Copts may have a spiritual life," Pope Shenouda said.

The human rights group Amnesty International has condemned incidents of killings of Christians in Egypt. Many have taken place in the southern province of Assiut, where clashes between Christians and Moslems erupted about four years ago and set off a spiral of violence which has claimed almost 1,000 lives.
The Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), the main Islamist militant organisation, has at times targeted Christians as part of its campaign for a stricter Islamic state in Egypt.
Loza said militant incidents aside, any suggestion that institutionalised religious discrimination and sectarian violence are rampant are an "exaggeration."
"Why have we become weak? I personally feel we have made ourselves a second-class community. Most of our young men have gone abroad," she said.
